newsitem.title: GERMANY: German aerospace sector pleads for govt support.
newsitem.headline: German aerospace sector pleads for govt support.

text.p: Germany's aerospace industry urged the Bonn government on Tuesday to commit itself to orders for major defence projects like the four-nation Eurofighter or risk jeopardising the sector's future.
"A decision must be taken on Eurofighter production this year. Anything else would have catastrophic results," Werner Heinzmann of the German Aerospace Industries Association said.

Germany has squeezed its defence budget as it fights to meet the debt and budget deficit limits set by the Maastricht treaty to qualify for European monetary union in 1999. Spending will be cut by 500 million marks ($330.7 million) to 46.6 billion marks in 1997.

At the same time Germany is assuming a higher international profile, breaking post-war taboos by sending soldiers to join United Nations peacekeeping forces in Bosnia, and pushing for a permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council.

Heinzmann, who is also on the board of Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG, called on Bonn to back other European defence projects such as the Tiger and NH90 helicopters, the Helios spy satellite and the so-called Future Large Aircraft.
"Policymakers must give this industry clear and reliable prospects and give a basis for long-term planning," he told a news conference.
Britain has already pledged to buy over 200 Eurofighters, to be built by a consortium grouping British Aerospace Plc, Dasa, Alenia SpA of Italy and Spain's CASA.
Germany has yet to make a firm order for the multi-purpose combat aircraft, although the government has said that there would be budget money for the project next year.

Heinzmann said that Germany was at a watershed and planned cuts could come as a further heavy blow after the number of jobs in the German armaments sector slumped to 120,000 from 280,000 in 1990 -- the year of German unification.
"We are not just talking of thousands of highly-qualified jobs and facilities, but an irreplaceable know-how which is at risk," he said.
-- Douglas Busvine, Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150 ($ = 1.512 German Marks)
